title: Still waters, rapid currents: Early labor market transformation under generative AI
key_facts: Researchers surveyed about 25,000 Danish workers (2024 round) in 11 AI-exposed occupations and linked answers to monthly administrative records through December 2024.
Headline result: no effect on earnings or hours, for chatbot users or for the firms that adopt them; estimates rule out differential earnings changes larger than 2%.
43% of workers in these occupations work for employers that encourage chatbot use; only 6% are prohibited.
Workplace use is changing jobs: new tasks such as overseeing AI output and integrating chatbots; 85% of users spend saved time on other job tasks.
No differential change in headcount, wage bills, hiring or separations at adopting workplaces.
Adopters worked about 4% of a full-time equivalent more hours in their latest occupation, which suggests they were more likely to switch jobs, mostly into IT support and clerical roles.
Switchers' earnings growth ran 12 percentage points ahead of other Danish workers.
Data end in December 2024 and cover Denmark only.
quote_evidence: The headline result is a precise null: no effects on earnings or hours, either for workers who use chatbots or for the firms that adopt them.
Beneath this still surface, however, work is already being substantially reorganized.
why_it_matters_hint: Early evidence shows AI is changing what jobs involve before it shows up in pay or hiring.
notes: Research article by the authors (not named in extracted text); Denmark only.
